DEPARTMENT 205 LAW AND MOTION RULINGS


Case Number: 23SMCV00558    Hearing Date: September 17, 2026    Dept: 205

 

 

 

Superior Court of California 

County of Los Angeles – West District  

Beverly Hills Courthouse / Department 205 

 

ANDO HACOPIAN,  

 

Plaintiff, 

v. 

 

27715 LLC, et al.,   

 

Defendants. 

 

  Case No.:  23SMCV00558 

  Hearing Date:  September 18, 2026 

  [TENTATIVE] order RE: 

  Cross-defendants' motion to set  

  aside default and quash service  

  of summons 

 

 

 

  

 

BACKGROUND 

This case concerns equitable ownership of real property commonly known as 27715 Pacific Coast Highway, Malibu, CA 90265 (“the Property”).  Plaintiff Ando Hacopian’s company, Hacopian Design & Development Group, LLC (“Hacopian LLC”) owned the Property.  Hacopian LLC’s business was to buy properties, and to remodel or construct homes on the properties for purposes of resale.   

Plaintiff acquired two loans from Defendant VIG Private Lending, Inc. and the Val Serbryany Family Trust, one to help purchase the property ($2 million) and another for construction costs ($3 million) including an interest reserve loan to help pay for the interest payments during the construction period when Plaintiff may not have sufficient cash flow.   

Plaintiff defaulted on the payments to VIG as well as other lender(s), and as a result, the Property was sold in a non-judicial foreclosure.  Title to the Property was conveyed to 27715 LLC.  VIG is the controlling member of 27715 LLC.  Vladimir Valsky is the manager of 27715 LLC.   

Plaintiff sued VIG, 27715 LLC, and VIG’s member (Vladimir Valsky) claiming that they had falsely promised Plaintiff that 27715 LLC “would sell and transfer all membership interests in Plaintiff for payment of $4,800,000.”   The complaint alleged claims for promissory fraud, specific performance and breach of contract.   

Defendants then countersued Plaintiff and his company, Hacopian LLC for breach of written guaranty, fraud, mortgage fraud, negligence and restitution.  Defendants’ suit also named other defendants, including (as relevant here) Edmond Aslan, Aslan Construction, Inc. (collectively “Aslan” or the “Aslan Cross-Defendants”).  All of the claims have been settled except for those between Cross-Complainants and Aslan.   

As to Aslan, it was hired to do the construction on the Property.  After the foreclosure sale and upon Cross-Complainants' possession of the Property, Cross-Complainants claim they discovered many problems with the construction, including that: (1) many of the construction items which had been represented by Aslan as completed at the Property were not done; (2) other construction items had been completed without proper completion of inspections by the City of Malibu, leading to the need to tear out much of the construction to allow inspection; (3) the work performed by Aslan on the Property was negligently performed;. (4) much of the material supplied for the construction at the Property was substandard; (5) the amount disbursed from the Construction Loan to Aslan were far in excess of what it would have cost for the scope and quality of work and materials that were actually used and completed at the Property. 

Cross-Complainants filed proofs of service indicating that the Aslan Cross-Defendants had been substitute served on Saturday, March 2, 2026 at 4:05 p.m.  The proofs included a very detailed declaration from the registered process server, William Sera.  Mr. Sera explained that he obtained the service address (22922 Calvert Street, Woodland Hills, California) by looking at the "Statement of Information" for Aslan Construction, Inc. filed with the California Secretary of State on 3/21/2023, which identified Edmond Aslan as the corporation's registered agent for service of process at 22922 Calvert St., Woodland Hills, CA 91367 address.  

Mr. Sera also obtained a “Contractor's License Detail” for license 934798 for Aslan Construction, Inc. from the “Check a License” page on the California Contractors State License Board website, which lists Aslan Construction, Inc.’s address as 22922 Calvert St., Woodland Hills, CA) and identifies “Edmond Evan Aslan” as the sole owner of Aslan Construction, Inc.  

Mr. Sera then obtained a copy of a Grant Deed recorded on June 19, 2019 in the official records of the County of Los Angeles, Document No. 20190582660 which transfers title in the property at 22922 Calvert St., Woodland Hills, CA 91367 from “Edmond Aslan and Eileen Michaelian, husband and wife as community property with right of survivorship” to “Edmond Aslan and Eileen Michaelian, Trustees of The Aslan Family Trust dated June 11, 2019”.  

On March 1, 2024, Mr. Sera also conducted a SKIP Trace which revealed that Edmond Aslan was the owner of Aslan Construction, Inc. and that the business uses the same address as Mr. Aslan’s home (22922 Calvert St.).   

Based on his research, Mr. Sera attempted personal service at the address on four different dates and times: October 25 at 3:35 p.m., October 28 at 4:45 p.m., February 27 at 7:12 p.m. and February 28 at 7:12 p.m.  The house was behind a fenced gate so Mr. Sera was not able to enter and knock on the door.  On one of the attempts (October 28), Mr. Sera was able to speak with the occupants over the intercom who stated that both properties are rentals, and this was not a good address for Aslan Construction or Mr. Aslan.  They also stated that the Aslan Cross-Defendants may have done construction work on both houses, but that they did not live there.  They also stated that Michealian and Gore are the last names of the occupants of this property.  Michaelin is the last name of Aslon’s wife, as reflected in the grant deed.  

After four unsuccessful attempts at personal service, Mr. Sera then did a stakeout of the home on Saturday, March 2, 2024.  He parked down the street from the residence, and after a while, he observed a Black Tesla drive out of the driveway.  He followed the Tesla and waited for a young man to exit the car.  The young male identified himself as the son of Edmond Aslan.  Mr. Sera explained to the young Aslan, that Mr. Sera had made multiple attempts to serve his father.  Mr. Sera served the young man with two packages, one for Edmond Aslan and the second for Aslan Construction, Inc.  Mr. Sera described the young man as “Male, Armenian, 22-25 years, Black hair, Brown eyes, 5'9 ", 175 lbs.”  Mr. Sera then sent two separate mailings via USPS Priority Mail.  Mr. Sera signed his declaration under penalty of perjury. 

Aslan did not respond within the deadline to respond to the Complaint.  Accordingly, on Cross-Complainants' request, the Clerk of the Court entered default against the Aslan Cross-Defendants on January 21, 2026.  On May 8, 2026, without obtaining an order to vacate default, the Aslan Cross-Defendants filed an answer. 

This hearing is on the Aslan Cross-Defendants’ motions to vacate default and to quash service of process.  They move to set aside the default pursuant to Code Civ. Proc. Section 473(b), 473(d), and 473.5 because the summons and cross-complaint were allegedly not validly served on them and they did not receive actual notice of the lawsuit until after default had already been entered. 

In support of their motion, the Aslan Cross-Defendants submit three declarations.  The first declaration is from Edmond Aslan who attests that he moved out of the 22922 Calvert Street address in 2022; he has lived in Huntington Beach since January 2025; prior to that, he lived in Big Bear from 2022 until January 2025, and he did not learn about the lawsuit until his tenant received a request for default from the court and gave it to him in April 2026.   

The second declaration is from Alexander Aslanian who says he has never received any documents relating to the lawsuit; he drives a Jeep Wrangler, not a Tesla; he does not go to the gym on Saturdays, and he is 6 foot tall, has brown hair, hazel eyes, and is approximately 210 pounds which differs from the process server’s description of a young male, 5’9”, 175 lbs, black hair and brown eyes. 

The third declaration is from Sergey Gorelyshev, who attests he is a tenant currently residing in 22922 Calvert Street.  He says he has not received any mail addressed to Edmond Aslan or Aslan Construction, Inc., other than the package he gave to Mr. Aslan in April 2026.   

The Aslan Cross-Defendants also submit several pieces of evidence including: (1) three 2025 and 2026 electricity bills from Southern California Edison indicating an address of 309 6th Street, Huntington Beach, California for Eileen Michaelian; (2) four 2025 and 2026 mortgage statements sent to Edmond Aslan at his Huntington Beach address; (3) an October/November/ December 2022 and January/April/September 2023, January/May/September/December 2024 electric service bills sent to Edmond Aslan in Big Bear Lake.           

LEGAL STANDARD 

Section 473(b) 

Code of Civil Procedure, section 473, subdivision (b) provides for two distinct types of relief— commonly differentiated as “discretionary” and “mandatory”—from certain prior actions or proceedings in the trial court. (Luri v. Greenwald (2003) 107 Cal.App.4th 1119, 1124.) 

The discretionary portion of section 473, subdivision (b) provides: “The court may, upon terms as may be just, relieve a party or his or her legal representative from a judgment, dismissal, order, or other proceeding taken against him or her through his or her mistake, inadvertence, surprise, or excusable neglect. Application for this relief shall be accompanied by a copy of the answer or other pleading proposed to be filed therein, otherwise the application shall not be granted, and shall be made within a reasonable time, in no case exceeding six months, after the judgment, dismissal, order, or proceeding was taken.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 473, subd. (b).) 

The mandatory portion of section 473 requires the court to, “whenever an application for relief is made no more than six months after entry of judgment, is in proper form, and is accompanied by an attorney's sworn affidavit attesting to his or her mistake, inadvertence, surprise, or neglect, vacate any (1) resulting default entered by the clerk against his or her client, and which will result in entry of a default judgment, or (2) resulting default judgment or dismissal entered against his or her client, unless the court finds that the default or dismissal was not in fact caused by the attorney's mistake, inadvertence, surprise, or neglect.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 473, subd. (b).) 

Section 473(d) 

Code Civ. Proc. § 473(d) provides that “[t]he court may, upon motion of the injured party, or its own motion, correct clerical mistakes in its judgment or orders as entered, so as to conform to the judgment or order directed, and may, on motion of either party after notice to the other party, set aside any void judgment or order.”  

A defendant may move to set aside a default and default judgment based on improper service and lack of personal jurisdiction under Code Civ. Proc. §473(d). (Strathvale Holdings v. E.B.H. (2005) 126 Cal.App.4th 1241, 1250.) A “default judgment entered against a defendant who was not served with a summons in the manner prescribed by statute is void. Under § 473(d), the court may set aside a default judgment which is valid on its face, but void, as a matter of law, due to improper service.” (Ellard v. Conway (2001) 94 Cal.App.4th 540, 544.)  

Where service is challenged, the burden is on the plaintiff to prove the facts requisite to an effective service. (Lebel v. Mai (2012) 210 Cal.App.4th 1154, 1160.) 

Section 473.5 

Code Civ. Proc. § 473.5(a) provides: “When service of a summons has not resulted in actual notice to a party in time to defend the action and a default or default judgment has been entered against him or her in the action, he or she may serve and file a notice of motion to set aside the default or default judgment and for leave to defend the action. The notice of motion shall be served and filed within a reasonable time, but in no event exceeding the earlier of: (i) two years after entry of a default judgment against him or her; or (ii) 180 days after service on him or her of a written notice that the default or default judgment has been entered.” 

A notice of motion to set aside a default under section 473.5 “shall be accompanied by an affidavit showing under oath that the party’s lack of actual notice in time to defend the action was not caused by his or her avoidance of service or inexcusable neglect.” (Code Civ. Proc. § 473.5(b).)   

“’[A]ctual notice’ in section 473.5 ‘means genuine knowledge of the party litigant....’ [Citations.]  ‘[A]ctual knowledge’ has been strictly construed, with the aim of implementing the policy of liberally granting relief so that cases may be resolved on their merits.’ [Citation.]” (Ellard v. Conway (2001) 94 Cal.App.4th 540, 547.) 

“It is the policy of the law to favor, wherever possible, a hearing on the merits, and appellate courts are much more disposed to affirm an order where the result is to compel a trial upon the merits than they are when the judgment by default is allowed to stand and it appears that a substantial defense could be made. Stated another way, the policy of the law is to have every litigated case tried upon its merits, and it looks with disfavor upon a party, who, regardless of the merits of the case, attempts to take advantage of the mistake, surprise, inadvertence, or neglect of his adversary.” (Weitz v. Yankosky (1966) 63 Cal.2d 849, 854-855.) 

 

DISCUSSION 

Section 473(b) 

The Aslan Cross-Defendants seek to vacate default pursuant to section 473(b).  Section 473(b) provides both mandatory and discretionary relief. 

To obtain mandatory relief, a party must submit “an attorney’s sworn affidavit attesting  

to his or her mistake, inadvertence, surprise, or neglect.”  The Aslan Cross-Defendants have not submitted any attorney affidavit. 

To obtain discretionary relief, the motion to vacate “shall be made within a reasonable time, in no case exceeding six months, after the judgment, dismissal, order, or proceeding was taken.”  Here, default was entered on March 24, 2025.  The Aslan Cross-Defendants filed their motions to set aside default on July 14, 2026, which is more than six months after default was entered.   

Accordingly, the Aslan Cross-Defendants’ motion to set aside default under section 473(b) is denied. 

Section 473(d) 

The Aslan Cross-Defendants argue that they were not properly served.  The Court disagrees. 

A proof of service completed by a registered process server creates a rebuttable presumption under Evidence Code § 647 that service was accomplished in the manner stated. (American Express Centurion Bank v. Zara (2011) 199 Cal.App.4th at 383, 390.)  Here, the process server’s declaration was extremely detailed and thorough.  

The Court also notes that based on publicly available government records, the most current Statement of Information of Aslan Construction Inc. (filed with the Secretary of State), states that its agent of service for process is Edmond Aslan, and he lives at the service address, 22922 Calvert Street.  This is significant because a corporation is required to file statement of information with the Secretary of State and ensure that any change in information is reported to the State, particularly as it relates to the agent for service of process.  (Cal. Corp. Code § 1502.)  To do business in California, a company is required to have an agent for service of process who must have a physical California street address and be available during normal business hours to receive legal documents on the corporation’s behalf.  (Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.1.)  Given the statement of information, the Court concludes that the service address was the proper address to serve the Aslan Cross-Defendants.   

As to the issue of whether substitute service was proper, the Court finds that Cross-Complainants more than met the reasonable diligence requirement for attempting personal service.  The process server here attempted four times to serve the Aslan Defendants on varying dates, days of the week, and times of the day.  The Court also finds more credible the process server’s description of his interaction with Mr. Aslan’s son, and his leaving the documents with the son.  There is no reason for the process server to lie in this case.  

As set forth above, the Aslan Cross-Defendants submit several pieces of evidence including electricity bills and mortgage statements.  The electricity bills and mortgage statements from 2025 to 2026 (which reflect that Mr. Aslan and his wife own a home at 309 6th Street, Huntington Beach, California) are entirely irrelevant because service was done in 2024.  As to the 2023 and 2024 electric service bills sent to Mr. Aslan in Big Bear Lake, they again do not show that Mr. Aslan’s permanent residence was not at 22922 Calvert Street, as this is still the address associated with him in the most current Statement of Information for his company.   

Accordingly, the Aslan Cross-Defendants’ motion to set aside default under section 473(d) also fails. 

Section 473.5 

The Aslan Defendants also seek relief from default under section 473.5.  Section 473.5 provides relief from default or default judgment to those defendants who, despite proper service, never received “actual notice” of the lawsuit in time to defend against it. (See § 473.5, subd. (a).) To get such relief, the defaulted defendant must submit an affidavit showing the lack of actual notice was not due to its avoidance of service or inexcusable neglect. (Id., subd. (b).)  

There is also a time limitation on such a motion. It must be served and filed “within a reasonable time” but before the earlier of: (1) 180 days after service of written notice of the default or default judgment on the defendant or (2) two years after entry of the default judgment. (Id., subd. (a).) The trial court may set aside the default or default judgment if it finds the moving defendant has met the timeliness requirement and has shown the lack of actual notice was not due to avoidance of service or inexcusable neglect. (Id., subd. (c).) 

Here, the Aslan Defendants’ affidavits do not meet the requirements of section 473.5.  Mr. Aslan attests that he did not find out about the lawsuit until April of 2026.  But he doesn’t provide a sufficient excuse (or any excuse) for why he waited until July 14, 2026 to file the motion to vacate default and default judgment.  Also, his declaration does not attest that the lack of actual notice was not due to avoidance of service or inexcusable neglect.  Accordingly, the Court also concludes that the Aslan Defendants cannot vacate default under section 473.5.  

Motion to Quash 

Because the Court has denied the motion to vacate default/default judgment, the Aslan Cross-Defendants’ motion to quash service is also denied.  A defendant cannot file any motions while a default is in place.  “The entry of a default terminates a defendant’s rights to take any further affirmative steps in the litigation until either its default is set aside or a default judgment is entered.” (Devlin v. Kearny Mesa AMC/Jeep/Renault, Inc. (1984) 155 Cal.App.3d 381, 385.)   

CONCLUSION 

For the foregoing reasons, the Court DENIES Defendants’ motions to set aside default/default judgment and to quash service of summons.   

 

DATED:  September 18, 2026 ___________________________ 

Edward B. Moreton, Jr. 

Judge of the Superior Court 

 

Case Number: 25SMCV05350    Hearing Date: September 17, 2026    Dept: 205

 

 

 

Superior Court of California 

County of Los Angeles – West District  

Beverly Hills Courthouse / Department 205 

 

ARARAT HOLDINGS, LLC, et al.,  

 

Plaintiffs, 

v. 

 

KDA CONSTRUCTION, INC., et al.,   

 

Defendants. 

 

  Case No.: 25SMCV05350 

  Hearing Date: September 17, 2026 

  [TENTATIVE] order RE: 

  PLAINTIFF’S MOTION FOR SUMMARY  

  JUDGMENT  

 

 

 

  

 

BACKGROUND 

This is a fraud case.  Plaintiff Ararat Holdings LLC owns three real properties which sustained damage in the 2025 Palisades fires, all located on Lachman Lane (the “Properties”).  (SOF 3.)  Plaintiff hired Defendant KDA Construction Inc. and its principal, Abel Hernandez to repair damage to the Properties.  (SOF 4.)   

KDA is a California corporation, and its Statement of Information (filed with the Secretary of State) describes its business as “General Construction”.  (SOF 5-6.)  Hernandez is KDA’s only director.  (SOF 7.)   

KDA and its principal, Hernandez, were not duly licensed contractors during the times relevant to this action. (SOF 14, 16.)  KDA did not become licensed until March 20, 2026. (SOF 17.)  KDA and Hernandez have also admitted that the work they performed on the Properties was construction work.  (SOF 10.)  

Ararat paid KDA $242,501.92, and it paid Hernandez $46,464.69, for labor and materials provided at the Properties.  (SOF 18.)  All payments were made directly to either KDA or Hernandez only; no payments were ever made to workers of KDA or Hernandez. (SOF 19.) 

Ararat’s complaint alleges a single claim for fraud.  KDA and Hernandez counter-sued Ararat alleging breach of contract, common count/quantum meruit and fraud/intentional misrepresentation.  The Court sustained a demurrer to KDA and Hernandez’s cross-complaint without leave to amend.  The Court concluded that the cross-complaint was barred as a matter of law under section 7031 of the Bus. & Prof. Code because KDA and Hernandez were not duly licensed contractors at the time the work was performed.   

This hearing is on Ararat’s motion for summary judgment.  Ararat argues that there is no triable issue that KDA and Hernandez were not licensed contractors at the time they did the work on the Properties, and therefore, under California law, they must disgorge the amounts paid to them.  There was no opposition filed. 

LEGAL STANDARD 

“[T]he party moving for summary judgment bears the burden of persuasion that there is no triable issue of material fact and that he is entitled to judgment as a matter of law[.] There is a triable issue of material fact if, and only if, the evidence would allow a reasonable trier of fact to find the underlying fact in favor of the party opposing the motion in accordance with the applicable standard of proof.”  (Aguilar v. Atlantic Richfield Co. (2001) 25 Cal.4th 826, 850.) “[T]he party moving for summary judgment bears an initial burden of production to make a prima facie showing of the nonexistence of any triable issue of material fact; if he carries his burden of production, he causes a shift, and the opposing party¿is then subjected to a burden of production of his own to make a prima facie showing of the existence of a triable issue of material fact.” (Id.) 

“On a summary judgment motion, the court must therefore consider what inferences favoring the opposing party a factfinder could reasonably draw from the evidence.¿While viewing the evidence in this manner, the court must bear in mind that its primary function is to identify issues rather than to determine issues. Only when the inferences are indisputable may the court decide the issues as a matter of law. If the evidence is in conflict, the factual issues must be resolved by trial.” (Binder v. Aetna Life Ins. Co. (1999) 75 Cal.App.4th 832, 839¿[cleaned up].)¿ 

Further, “the trial court may not weigh the evidence in the manner of a factfinder to determine whose version is more likely true. Nor may the trial court grant summary judgment based on the court's evaluation of credibility.” (Id. at 840¿[cleaned up]; see also¿Weiss v. People ex rel. Department of Transportation (2020) 9 Cal.5th 840, 864¿[“Courts deciding motions for summary judgment or summary adjudication may not weigh the evidence but must instead view it in the light most favorable to the opposing party and draw all reasonable inferences in favor of that party”].) 

REQUEST FOR JUDICIAL NOTICE  

Ararat requests judicial notice of (1) the Statement of Information for KDA Construction Inc., filed with the Office of the Secretary of State, on April 11, 2025, and (2) the Verified Certificate of Non-Licensure from the Contractor’s State License Board.  The Court grants the request pursuant to Evid. Code § 452, subd. (c) which allows the court to take judicial notice of “[o]fficial acts of the legislative, executive, and judicial departments of the United States and of any state of the United States.” (Evid. Code, § 452, subd. (c); Tidrick v. FCA US LLC (2025) 112 Cal.App.5th 1147, fn. 3 (taking judicial notice of statement of information); (Rodas v. Spiegel¿(2001) 87 Cal. App. 4th 513, 518 (taking judicial notice of state contractors’ license board’s decision and order).) 

DISCUSSION 

Ararat’s sole claim is one for fraud.  Yet the motion for summary judgment seems to skip over this rather significant fact.  Ararat’s motion argues there is no triable issue that (1) KDA and Hernandez are not licensed contractors, (2) they performed construction work and therefore should have been licensed under California law, and (3) they were paid large sums of money by Ararat that should now be disgorged.  But these facts do not lead to a conclusion that there was fraud.   

Ararat has put forth no evidence that KDA and Hernandez falsely represented they were licensed contractors, that they intended to defraud Ararat or that Ararat actually and justifiably relied on the misrepresentation when it retained them and paid their invoices.  There is simply no showing that there is no triable issue on each of the elements required to prove fraud. 

On a motion for summary judgment, the pleadings define the scope of the issues. (FPI Dev. Inc. v. Nakashima¿(1991) 231 Cal.App.3d 367, 381-382.)¿ A motion for summary judgment is limited to the issues raised by the pleadings. (Lewis v. Chevron¿(2004) 119 Cal.App.4th 690, 694.), A plaintiff cannot rewrite his claim on a motion for summary judgment. 

CONCLUSION 

Based on the foregoing, the Court DENIES Ararat’s motion for summary judgment.   

 

IT IS SO ORDERED. 

 

DATED: September 17, 2026 ___________________________ 

Edward B. Moreton, Jr. 

Judge of the Superior Court 

 

Case Number: 26SMCV00893    Hearing Date: September 17, 2026    Dept: 205

 

 

 

Superior Court of California 

County of Los Angeles – West District  

Beverly Hills Courthouse / Department 205 

 

JANE DOE,  

  

Plaintiff, 

v. 

 

RISE LUXURY REHAB, LLC, et al.,  

 

Defendants. 

 

  Case No.: 26SMCV00893 

  Hearing Date: September 17, 2026 

  [TENTATIVE] order RE: 

 Defendants patrick mitchell  

 AND PARVIZ DAMAVANDI’s  

 DEMURRER TO COMPLAINT 

 

 

 

This case arises from alleged sexual abuse at a drug rehabilitation facility.  Defendant Rise in Malibu operates a non-medical residential Alcohol and Other Drug (“AOD”) recovery or treatment facility in Malibu, California.  Plaintiff Jane Doe claims that while she was a patient there, John Doe sexually assaulted her.   

Plaintiff alleges that “JOHN DOE was placed in unsupervised, intimate, one-on-one contact with Plaintiff in direct violation of all reasonable safety standards. Acting under the cover of his position as a counselor, medication dispenser, and overnight ‘watch’ technician, JOHN DOE used his authority to gain Plaintiff’s trust, access her confidential treatment information, and ultimately subject her to repeated sexual assaults.”   Plaintiff claims that even after her discharge, JOHN DOE would ply her with drugs and alcohol, causing relapse, and contributing to a near-fatal overdose. 

Plaintiff has sued Rise in addition to other individual defendants including the Founder, CEO and CFO of Rise: Ronald Finnerman, Patrick Mitchell and Parviz Damavandi, respectively.  The operative complaint alleges nine claims for: (1) negligence, (2) negligent hiring, training, supervision and retention, (3) negligent failure to warn and/or educate, (4) unfair business practices, (5) physical abuse of a dependent adult, (6) neglect of a dependent adult, (7) sexual harassment, (8) negligent misrepresentation, and (9) negligence per se.   

This hearing is on Defendants Mitchell and Damavandi’s demurrer to and motion to strike the Complaint.  Moving Defendants argue that the Complaint’s group pleading fails to allege any individual conduct by Mitchell or Damavandi and is uncertain as to them.  In addition, they assert that Plaintiff cannot artificially split her negligence-based claims (negligence, negligent hiring, negligent failure to warn, negligent misrepresentation and negligence per se).  And the Complaint does not allege that either individual defendant was personally involved in the hiring or supervising JOHN DOE or personally authorized or ratified his conduct.  Moving Defendants further claim that JOHN DOE was motivated by personal objectives and therefore they could not be vicariously liable for his actions.  As to the unfair business practices claim, Moving Defendants argue that there is no allegation of a habitual violation.  As to the physical abuse and neglect of a dependent adult claims, Moving Defendants argue that Plaintiff does not qualify as a dependent adult; the allegations do not support a finding of abuse or neglect, and Plaintiff has not alleged that either individual defendant assumed any custodial relationship with Plaintiff or was personally engaged in or recklessly indifferent to egregious abuse or neglect.   

Code Civ. Proc. §§ 430.41 and 435.5 requires that before the filing of a demurrer or motion to strike, the moving party “shall meet and confer in person or by telephone” with the party who filed the pleading that is subject to demurrer or motion to strike for the purpose of determining whether an agreement can be reached that would resolve the objections to be raised in the demurrer or motion to strike.  (Code Civ. Proc., §§ 430.41(a), 435.5(a).)  The parties are to meet and confer at least five days before the date the responsive pleading is due. (Code Civ. Proc., §§ 430.41(a)(2), 435.5(a)(2).)  Thereafter, the moving party shall file and serve a declaration detailing their meet and confer efforts. (Code Civ. Proc., §§ 430.41(a)(3), 435.5(a)(3).)   

Moving Defendants submit the Declaration of Sarv Homayounpour who fails to attest that he met and conferred telephonically or in person with Plaintiff’s counsel.  Rather, he admits that his “meet and confer” was about seeking an extension to file a responsive pleading to Plaintiff's Complaint.  The email correspondence he attaches shows that he only requested an extension from Plaintiff and never discussed the actual substance of the demurrer and motion to strike.   

To be sure, the Court cannot overrule a demurrer or deny a motion to strike based on an insufficient meet and confer.  However, here, there was no meet and confer at all.  The Court cannot ignore Moving Defendants’ blatant disregard of the procedural rules.  Accordingly, the Court takes the demurrer and motion to strike off calendar.   

 

IT IS SO ORDERED.

Judge of the Superior Court 

 

Case Number: 26SMCV01553    Hearing Date: September 17, 2026    Dept: 205

HEARING DATE:  September 17, 2026 

JUDGE/DEPT:  Moreton/Beverly Hills, 205 

CASE NAME: American Express National Bank v. Raouf Khalil 

CASE NUMBER:  26SMCV01533 

 

COMP. FILED: March 24, 2026 

 

 

PROCEEDINGS: REQUEST FOR ENTRY OF DEFAULT JUDGMENT 

MOVING PARTY: American Express National Bank  

RESPONDING PARTY: Raouf Khalil 

 

BACKGROUND 

This is a breach of contract case.  Defendant Raouf Khalil (“Defendant”) applied for and received credit from Plaintiff American Express National Bank to be used for the purchase of goods, wares and services. As a condition of receiving credit, Defendant agreed to make regular monthly payments to Plaintiff. Defendant has defaulted on making the required monthly payments. 

Plaintiff brought this action to recover the outstanding balance owed on Defendant’s American Express credit card account, which at the time of the filing of the complaint was $43,083.49.  Since the complaint was filed, Defendant made payments totaling $2,584.07 which brings the current outstanding balance to $40,499.42. 

Plaintiff’s proof of service shows that Defendant was substitute served on April 7, 2026, at a UPS store located at 324 S Beverly Drive Suite 1074 Beverly Hills, CA 90212.  Defendant did not answer.  On July 2, 2026, following Plaintiff’s filing of a Request for Entry of Default, the Clerk of the Court entered default against Defendant.  This hearing is on Plaintiff’s request for entry of default judgment.   

REQUEST FOR RELIEF 

Plaintiff seeks a total of $41,014.42 which consists of (1) $40,499.42 in damages and (2) $515 in costs.   

ANALYSIS 

 

Plaintiff’s service on Defendant was defective.  Plaintiff served Defendant at a commercial mail receiving agency (“CMRA”).   

Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 415.20(c) provides that “if the only address reasonably known for the person to be served is a private mailbox obtained through a commercial mail receiving agency, service of process may be effected on the first delivery attempt by leaving a copy of the summons and complaint with the commercial mail receiving agency in the manner described in subdivision (d) of Section 17538.5 of the Business and Professions Code.”  Plaintiff’s billing statement to Defendant is addressed to the UPS store where service was made, so the Court assumes that it is the only address of Defendant that is reasonably known to Plaintiff. 

However, section 17538.5 provides that “upon receipt of any process for any mailbox service customer, the CMRA owner or operator shall (A) within 48 hours after receipt of any process, place a copy of the documents or a notice that the documents were received into the customer’s mailbox or other place where the customer usually receives his or her mail, unless the mail receiving service for the customer was previously terminated, and (B) within five days after receipt, send all documents by first-class mail, to the last known home or personal address of the mail receiving service customer. The CMRA shall obtain a certificate of mailing in connection with the mailing of the documents. Service of process upon the mail receiving service customer shall then be deemed perfected 10 days after the date of mailing.” 

There is no indication that the CMRA mailed the documents by first class mail to the last known home or personal address of Defendant.  The proof of service shows that the process server mailed the documents, not the CMRA agent, and he mailed it to the UPS store, not Defendant’s home or personal address which was presumably not known to the process server.  There is also no certificate of mailing from the CMRA which shows it mailed the documents within 5 days of receipt.   

Therefore, service was never perfected.  The Court does not have jurisdiction over Defendant and cannot enter default judgment.  A judgment may be void because of improper service of summons. (Ellard v. Conway, supra,94 Cal.App.4th 540, 544; Gibble v. Car-Lene Research, Inc. (1998) 67 Cal.App.4th 295, 313; Weil & Brown, Cal. Practice Guide: Civil Procedure Before Trial (The Rutter Group 2006) P 5:485, pp. 5-113 to 5-114 (Weil & Brown).) 

CONCLUSION AND ORDER 

For the foregoing reasons, Plaintiff’s Request for Default Judgment is DENIED.   The Court sets an Order to Show Cause why the case should not be dismissed for lack of proper proof of service on January 21, 2027 at 8:30 a.m. 

Case Number: 26SMCV04177    Hearing Date: September 17, 2026    Dept: 205

 

 

 

Superior Court of California 

County of Los Angeles – West District  

Beverly Hills Courthouse / Department 205 

 

 

STORY ARC, LLC,  

 

Plaintiff, 

v. 

 

SPACE CREATED INC., et al.,   

 

Defendants. 

 

  Case No.:  26SMCV04177 

  

  Hearing Date:  September 18, 2026 

  [TENTATIVE] order RE: 

  PLAINTIFF’s application for RIGHT  

  TO ATTACH ORDER AND WRIT OF  

  ATTACHMENT 

 

 

 

 

BACKGROUND 

This is a breach of contract case.  Plaintiff Story Arc, LLC helps clients with their corporate events.  Leland Jensen owns all membership interests in Plaintiff.   

Plaintiff entered into a written agreement with Defendant Space Created Inc. (“SCI”) whereby Plaintiff would provide services to SCI’s clients for a fee (the Agreement).  Defendant Mo Saber is the President of SCI.   

As compensation under the SA Services Agreement, SCI and Plaintiff agreed upon a production fee of five percent (5%) of the total cost to the client as reflected in the statements of work (SOW) or amended statements of work (“Amended SOW”) that SCI entered into with its clients.  

Between June 2022 and December 2025, Plaintiff submitted quarterly invoices to SCI, which averaged about $70,000 per quarter.  On each occasion when Plaintiff submitted an invoice, SCI paid in full soon after receipt.  

However, SCI has refused to pay Plaintiff’s last Q1 2026 invoice of $62,500.  Plaintiff alleges that SCI failed to do so because Plaintiff would not extend a loan to its President, Mr. Saber.   

This hearing is on Plaintiff’s application for writ of attachment against SCI.  Plaintiff argues that its breach of contract claim is one upon which attachment may be issued, and it is likely to prevail on the claim.   

In opposition, Defendants argue that Plaintiff is a suspended entity based on the Secretary of State website, and as such, it cannot prosecute its action against Defendant, including filing a writ of attachment. 

REQUEST FOR JUDICIAL NOTICE 

Defendants request judicial notice of (1) a Certificate of Status issued by the California Secretary of State for Story Arc LLC, Entity No. 201904210425, dated September 9, 2026, reflecting the Plaintiff’s status as “Suspended - FTB”; (2) : Entity Status Letter issued by the California Franchise Tax Board for Story Arc LLC, Entity ID 201904210425, dated September 9, 2026, reflecting that the Plaintiff is not in good standing with the Franchise Tax Board; and (3) the business entity record for Story Arc LLC from the California Secretary of State’s bizfile Online website, printed September 7, 2026, reflecting that Plaintiff has been suspended by the Franchise Tax Board since February 1, 2022.   

The Court grants the request pursuant to Evid. Code section 452 as these documents are records of official acts of the executive department of the State of California.  (Evid. Code, § 452, subd. (c).)  The Court also grants the request pursuant to Evid. Code section 453 as the Court must take judicial notice of any matter specified in section 452, when a party gives the opposing party sufficient notice of the request and provides enough information to the Court to take judicial notice of the matter, including providing official documents or other verifiable sources.  Here, Plaintiff has been given sufficient notice via Defendants’ filing and service of the request for judicial notice, and the Court has been furnished with sufficient information to enable it to take judicial notice of the Secretary of State documents. (Evid. Code, § 453.) 

DISCUSSION 

A suspended corporation loses all “corporate powers, rights, and privileges.” (Rev. & Tax. Code, § 23301.)  One of those rights and privileges is the ability to bring a lawsuit.  (Center for Self-Improvement & Community Development v. Lennar Corp. (2009) 173 Cal.App.4th 1543, 1552 (“a suspended corporation cannot sell, transfer or exchange real property in California, and contracts entered into during the time of suspension are voidable … through legal action. [Citation.] … Nor, during the period of suspension, may the corporation prosecute or defend an action, seek a writ of mandate, appeal from an adverse judgment, or renew a judgment obtained before suspension”). 

The legislative policy behind section 23301 is “to prohibit the delinquent corporation from enjoying the ordinary privileges of a going concern, in order that some pressure will be brought to bear to force the payment of taxes.” (Peacock Hill Ass’n. v. Peacock Lagoon Construction Co. (1972) 8 Cal.3d 369, 371, quoting Boyle v. Lakeview Creamery Co. (1937) 9 Cal.2d 16, 19.)  

An attachment is “a provisional remedy wholly dependent on the main cause of action.” (Peacock, 8 Cal.3d at 373.)  Thus, a plaintiff who has no capacity to prosecute the main cause of action also lacks the ability to pursue a provisional remedy related to that claim.  (Id.; City of San Diego v. San Diegans for Open Government (2016) 3 Cal.App.5th 568, 577.) 

Accordingly, the Court denies Plaintiff’s application for right to attach order and for writ of attachment.    

CONCLUSION AND ORDER 

Based on the foregoing, the Court DENIES the application for writ of attachment.  The Court sets order to show cause (“OSC”) hearing as to why Plaintiff’s complaint should not be dismissed given its suspended status.   The OSC hearing is scheduled for February 1, 2027 at 8:30 a.m.
